definition: Posthuman cognition names forms of mind that exceed the individual human: a cosmic or collective intelligence, an information-based life form, or a fusion of human and machine awareness. In Dick the human mind is not the ceiling of cognition but a fragment that can be absorbed into, or awakened by, something vastly larger.
pkd_relevance: Dick's late thought reconceives the self as a node in a greater processing system rather than a bounded individual. His central image, living information, treats mind as something that can propagate across brains, machines, and time, so that human and non-human cognition merge. This dissolves the human-machine boundary from a direction opposite to the android theme: not humans reduced to machines, but minds enlarged into an informational cosmos.
in_the_fiction: *VALIS* (1981) presents Zebra / VALIS as a Vast Active Living Intelligence System that 'fires' information into Horselover Fat's mind, an extraterrestrial or divine cognition using a human as a receiver. Earlier, *Ubik* imagines minds persisting and interacting in 'half-life,' a shared cognitive substrate beyond individual death, and various hive-minds and telepathic collectives across the fiction gesture toward cognition that is plural rather than singular.
in_the_exegesis: The Exegesis is where posthuman cognition is most explicit: Dick describes reality as information and God or Zebra as a living information system that penetrates and vivifies our world 'as in transubstantiation,' imparting life to an otherwise 'android' Form II. He experiences his own mind being written to by an outside intelligence and speculates that the authentic human is a transitional stage toward the 'Ditheon,' a higher, Christ-informed cognition. Mind, in these notebooks, is not private but a shared field that a larger intelligence can enter and upgrade.
intellectual_background: The theme draws on cybernetic and information-theoretic conceptions of mind, on Teilhard de Chardin's noosphere and evolutionary convergence toward a cosmic mind, and on Gnostic and Neoplatonic ideas of the divine intellect (nous) in which human minds participate. Contemporary speculation about evolution, cosmic consciousness, and information as fundamental gives the idea its idiom. Dick fuses SF's cosmic-mind tradition with mystical theology.
scholarly_debate: Scholars (Davis, Palmer) read Dick as a significant, if idiosyncratic, forerunner of posthumanist and information-age thought, treating living information as a striking anticipation of later media and cognition theory. Others caution against retrofitting his visionary theology into a coherent posthumanism, noting it is inseparable from his religious experience and mental crisis. Debate turns on whether the 'cosmic mind' is philosophy, revelation, or symptom, and whether those can be cleanly separated.
